title: When Working Through Disagreement, Understanding Must Come Before Reasoning
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note argues that leaders' first instinct in a disagreement, to marshal data and defend their position, gets the order wrong. Citing relationship research, it holds that before reasoning can do any good the other person must feel their perspective has been understood. Strong disagreement, the note says, harms relationships only when people do not feel understood by the other side. Many disputes in close relationships are perpetual rather than solvable, because they rest on differing priorities and values, so they must be worked through rather than argued away. A team member who loses an argument but feels genuinely understood concludes that the leader values them. The note does not ask leaders to abandon analysis, but insists that reasoning lands best on ground that understanding has prepared. It closes by proposing a replacement question for the leader: not how to win the argument, but whether the other person knows their view is understood.
points: Before a leader offers reasoning, the other party has to feel understood, or the argument will be received as a directive to resist.
Research cited in the note finds that strong disagreement harms relationships only when people do not feel understood.
Many workplace and personal disputes are perpetual because they rest on values and priorities, so they must be discussed and worked through rather than won.
Someone who loses the argument but feels understood concludes the leader values them, which protects the relationship.
The leader's first question should shift from how to win the argument to whether the other person knows the leader understands theirs.
quotes: Research on relationships suggests this instinct gets it wrong. Before reasoning can do any good, the other person must feel that their perspective has been understood.
Studies show that such disputes harm relationships only when people do not feel understood by the other side. When people feel understood, strong disagreement does no measurable harm.
In close relationships, inside and outside the workplace, many disputes are perpetual rather than solvable. The disagreements reside in the priorities people privilege and the values they hold.
Feeling understood signals that the leader is invested in the relationship. A team member who loses an argument but feels genuinely understood concludes the leader values them.

A well-built case presented to a team that feels unheard lands as a directive to be resisted. The same case presented to a team that feels understood is heard as a contribution to solving a shared problem.
The lesson for leaders is simple. In any disagreement, a leader’s first question should not be “How do I win this argument?” but “Do they know I understand theirs?
Arguments may win the point, but understanding wins the person. Leaders need both.
